proof.criterion: A2/A3/A5: a hub that runs a listener and is given no tailnet name is refused before anything registers; a tailnet name outside one label under ts.net is refused; a seed in the tailnet name or in any address entry is refused naming the input and never echoing the value.
proof.surface: The operator's surface — the hub refusing its inputs while Pulumi previews it (gcp.CloudConfigOf → newSettings → resolveListener, the path Construct takes before it registers anything), with a real nkey seed generated by nkeys.CreateUser().
proof.observed: Refused, each before any registration: a listener with no tailnetDnsName (`tailnetDnsName is required for a hub with a listener: …`); `ts.net` alone, `example-tailnet.net` and `Example-Tailnet.ts.net` (`tailnetDnsName %q must match ^[a-z0-9](?:[a-z0-9-]{0,61}[a-z0-9])?\.ts\.net$`); an entry with a port, a scheme, a wildcard, a comma, a trailing space, and an empty entry, each as `listener.allowedHosts[0] is "…": want a host name or address with no port, scheme or path`; a bad second entry as `listener.allowedHosts[1]`, the operator's own index, which is the simplify finding's whole point; a real seed as tailnetDnsName, as allowedHosts[0] and as allowedHosts[1], each `… : an nkey user seed, which is never an input of the hub (not echoed)`, with the seed absent from the message (asserted, not eyeballed). The refusal texts quoted in packages/envoy/infra/docs/nats-hub.md match what the code emits, index and all.
proof.negativeControl: A hub with tailnetDnsName set and no listener builds (no refusal), and a hub with neither builds too, so the refusal is scoped to the configuration that would otherwise serve nobody.

proof.criterion: A4: each further address is refused in exactly the cases the listener refuses one at boot, and the two rules cannot drift apart silently.
proof.surface: Differential run of the two rules over a generated corpus rather than the hand-written table the shipped agreement test uses: core.CheckAllowedHosts against the listener's own config.Load, 23,630 entries (every string of length 1–3 over `ab9.-:[]_*/ %@\t`, 20,000 random length-4–9 strings, and structured names: bracketed and bare IPv6, IPv4, trailing dot, upper case, punycode, non-ASCII, 300-character label, 100-label name).
proof.observed: Zero entries in the dangerous direction — none that core accepts and the listener refuses, which is the direction that deploys a hub whose listener cannot boot. 165 in the safe direction, all one class: entries with surrounding whitespace or an empty entry, which the listener's parseAllowedHosts trims or skips and core refuses outright. That strictness is right rather than wrong — a space inside an entry would be rendered into the unit's `docker run … -e ENVOY_ALLOWED_HOSTS=a b` and split the argument — but it is one class wider than 'exactly', and the shipped agreement test's table holds no whitespace row, so nothing pins the asymmetry either way. Recorded for the reviewer, not as a failure: nothing breaks, the deploy stops at preview with the entry quoted.
proof.negativeControl: The corpus's own accepted names (example-hub.example-tailnet.ts.net, [2001:db8::1], 192.0.2.7, a trailing-dot name) pass both rules, so the run is not one that refuses everything.
